objection: Didn’t Jesus say, ‘The Father is greater than I’—and call him the only true God?
answer:
Wa alaikum as-salam, and thank you for pressing this honestly—these two texts deserve a real answer, not a dodge.

On John 14:28: Jesus speaks these words as the incarnate Son, having taken the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7), on His way to the cross. The Fathers rightly distinguished statements Christ makes according to the economy of His incarnation from statements about His eternal essence. As man, sent by the Father, obedient unto death, He can truly say the Father is greater in the order of mission—just as a son dispatched by his father to accomplish a task can call the sender "greater" without being of a different nature. This coheres with the eternal relation of Father and Son itself: the Son is begotten of the Father, an order of origin, not an order of inferiority. The same Gospel that records "the Father is greater than I" opens by declaring "the Word was God" (John 1:1) and closes with Thomas confessing the risen Christ as "my Lord and my God" (John 20:28). John is not confused; he holds both truths together deliberately.

On John 17:3: in that very prayer, Jesus has just asked the Father to glorify Him with the glory He had with the Father "before the world was" (John 17:5)—language no mere creature could use. Calling the Father "the only true God" distinguishes the Father from the Son personally; it does not exclude the Son from the divine identity any more than John 1:1's "the Word was with God, and the Word was God" is self-contradictory. Christ prays as true man, according to His assumed humanity, even while remaining, according to His divinity, the eternal Word through whom all things were made. He is not praying to Himself in some confused sense; the Son addresses the Father, distinct in person, one in essence—which is exactly the Trinitarian claim, not a denial of it.

So these verses, read in their Johannine context, do not overturn "my Lord and my God"—they presuppose the very distinction of persons within one God that makes sense of the whole Gospel, cross to resurrection.

transcript.content: *Assalamu alaikum.* This is the clearest proof that Jesus himself denied his own divinity. In John 14:28, he says plainly, "The Father is greater than I"—not equal, not one substance, but *greater*. And then in John 17:3, in his own prayer, he calls God "the only true God" (*al-ilah al-haq*). If Jesus were God, how could he say this? How could he pray to himself, depend upon God, and teach his followers that the Father alone is the only true God? These are his own words—if you trust the Gospels at all, you must reckon with what he actually said about himself.
